newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Language in the workplace an increasing worry.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Language in the workplace an increasing worry.

text.p: Natalie Preston thought she would have a good chance at landing a marketing or communications job in Miami when she decided to leave a position in nearby Fort Myers in 1995.

A Florida native with a master's degree, contacts in the city and two years of solid work experience, the 27-year-old knew that service businesses in Miami were thriving, as companies opened offices and expanded.
But what Preston said she did not count on was how many jobs in Miami seemed barred to anyone who did not speak Spanish as well as English.
"I felt like I was seriously handicapped just knowing the English language," she said. "I was amazed at the level of jobs that required you to speak more than one language."
Those jobs were not just positions requiring international travel or contact with Latin American visitors, but jobs in public relations, writing and even retail buying, she said.
Eventually, Preston gave up on Miami, and took a communications job at Michigan State University in East Lansing, Michigan.
LANGUAGE DEBATE DIVIDES U.S WORKPLACES

Preston's experience was just one element in a language debate that divides U.S. workplaces, with workers more comfortable in Spanish angered by employers who demand they speak only English, and workers more comfortable in English annoyed by colleagues speaking other languages around them.

In greater Miami, where an estimated 60 percent of residents were born outside the United States and some one million people speak Spanish at home, outnumbering those who speak English, resentment runs deep.

In February, participants in "Black Out '97," an economic empowerment rally in downtown Miami said the refusal of Latin Americans to speak English has added another layer of bias to what they already face because of their skin colour.

Thomas Brookins, a corrections worker, said he had moved away to seek a better life, calling Miami the most difficult place for blacks in Florida. "It is because of the hold that the Latins have on the community," he said.
The Spanish American League Against Discrimination, a Miami advocacy group, said it takes dozens of calls weekly from Spanish speakers alleging discrimination because of their language or accents.
A row blew up in after George Batchelor, president of Miami-based International Air Leases, threatened to punish Spanish speakers in a memorandum banning Spanish at work.

"I will continue to pay my employees in American money, not pesos, but unless there is an immediate and continuing improvement, I intend to cut all vacation time in half," Batchelor, wrote, although he later apologised and said no one had been penalised for speaking Spanish.

Last year, investigators questioned whether workers at a the Miami facility of an aircraft maintenance firm questioned in connection with the fatal ValuJet air crash that May, had known English well enough to perform their jobs safely.

A poll published in the Miami Herald on April 25 showed that 62 percent of non-Hispanics in the Miami area felt employers have the right to demand that all staff speak only English at work, something believed by only 21 percent of Hispanics.

And 65 percent of non-Hispanics felt it was rude for bi-lingual people to speak to one another in front of fellow workers in a language they could not understand. Only 48 percent percent of Hispanics agreed.
PREPARING FOR MULTI-LINGUAL REALITY

Experts said Americans should put emotions aside and be prepared for a multi-lingual reality as more people speak more than one language and international trade becomes an increasingly important component of the U.S. economy.

In 1990, census figures showed that more than 17 million U.S. residents spoke Spanish, a number that experts said has risen, especially in states such as California, Texas, Florida, New Jersey and New York.

"The job market is recognising that it can demand bilingual skills and find applicants who qualify," said Jeff Wood, director of Career Development and Alumni at the Monterey Institute of International Studies in California. "There is a slight shift from bilingualism being a "plus" for an applicant to it being a "must have."

"In New York, there are 115 languages spoken daily...If you talk to the people at AT&T, they say they pride themselves on the fact that they speak 143 languages," said Professor Patricio Lerzundi, who heads a new Multilingual Journalism Programme at the City University of New York.
"Not just in the field of communications, but in most fields, it is essential that people speak other languages," he said.
